hlido_opinion.headline: A skills registry that scores whether a skill actually RUNS, not just whether it matches — the right idea, with a verification funnel that deserves more scrutiny than the headline number.
hlido_opinion.body: Hlido's automated public-surface checks recorded no passes on this run even though the page rendered and was captured in full, so the score reflects what our checks could VERIFY, not a judgement that the product is weak. Read the score as low confidence pending a re-test, and the notes below as what the captured surface says about itself. SkillsVote is a discovery and recommendation layer for agent skills, and its central insight is one the registry space mostly ignores: being findable is not the same as being runnable. The captured surface says it constructs real tasks from each skill and validates them in a controlled environment specifically to prevent the case where a skill is searchable, downloadable, and then does not work — and that each skill carries its environment requirements, permission scope, external dependencies and quality metrics so an agent can decide whether to call it at all before calling it. That is a materially more useful contract than a package index, and it is close to what Hlido argues about agents generally. The funnel it publishes is also the most informative thing on the page, and it reads against the headline: 1,681,615 skills indexed, 794,617+ verified, 322,930 passing quality assessment, 36,616 featured. So roughly 19% clear quality assessment and about 2% are featured — the 1.68M figure in the headline is an index size, not a supply of usable skills, and the page leads with the large number. The loop design is sound: vector retrieval for intent rather than keywords, task-description-to-skill-set recommendation with usage guidance rather than bare metadata, and post-execution feedback where the agent reports which skills it actually used plus a trace summary, feeding back into ranking. Access is via MCP, an OpenAgent SDK and a CLI, with plugin paths into Codex and Claude Code, and skills are stated to be signature-reviewed with version pinning. The interface is Chinese-only, requires login and an approved API key, and no verification methodology is published — which is the gap, since verification is the entire differentiator.

tier_rationale: FADING (50) is a measurement verdict: all required public-surface checks failed on this run, so the funnel figures, the verification process, the MCP surface and the signature review are unconfirmed by us. A product whose differentiator is verification, publishing no verification methodology, is precisely what a register must decline to credit until measured — a re-test is queued. It is not lower because the captured surface is specific, publishes a funnel that works against its own headline, and documents a real integration path.
what_it_does_well: Verifies whether a skill actually RUNS, not just whether it matches a query — the gap most registries ignore
Publishes environment requirements, permission scope, dependencies and quality metrics per skill, pre-call
Publishes the full funnel (1.68M indexed → 795k verified → 323k quality-passing → 37k featured) rather than one number
Feedback loop closes on execution: the agent reports which skills it used plus a trace summary, feeding ranking
Vector retrieval for intent rather than keyword matching, so a skill is findable without knowing its name
Multiple access paths — MCP, OpenAgent SDK and CLI — plus plugin integration into Codex and Claude Code
Skills stated to be signature-reviewed with version pinning
what_it_fails_at: All required public-surface checks failed on this run — nothing below is independently verified by us
No verification methodology published, which is the whole differentiator
The headline leads with 1.68M indexed skills while only ~19% pass quality assessment and ~2% are featured
Interface and documentation are Chinese-only with no English surface
Requires login and an approved API key before any capability can be assessed
No pricing, rate limits or availability commitment for a service agents would call at runtime
'Signature-reviewed' is asserted with no detail on who signs or what the review covers
best_for: Agent frameworks needing runtime skill discovery with a pre-call capability contract
Chinese-language agent developers (the only supported interface language)
Teams wanting execution feedback to improve skill selection over time
Codex or Claude Code users wanting a plugin-based skill source
not_recommended_for: Non-Chinese-reading developers — there is no English surface
Production dependencies needing published availability or rate limits
Anyone who needs the verification claims substantiated before trusting a skill at runtime
Teams preferring a curated, small, auditable skill set over a 1.68M index
red_flags: The differentiator is verification, and no verification methodology is published — only aggregate counts
Headline figure is an index size (1,681,615) while the same page shows ~19% passing quality assessment and ~2% featured; the leading number overstates usable supply
All required public-surface checks failed on this run while the page rendered fully — the score reflects unverified claims, not measured weakness; a re-test is queued

compared_to.verdict_diff: LangChain ships a large curated set of tools and integrations maintained in one repository. SkillsVote indexes a vastly larger third-party pool and claims to tell you which entries actually run. LangChain for a maintained, auditable set; SkillsVote for breadth plus a runnability claim you cannot yet verify.
Agno is an agent framework with its own curated toolkits. SkillsVote is not a framework but a discovery and recommendation service a framework calls. Complementary rather than competing.

A curated skills library offers a small, inspectable set. SkillsVote offers a 1.68M index with an automated quality funnel on top. Curation versus scale-plus-filtering — and the filter's method is not published.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Explicitly built for agent-to-agent use: MCP, an OpenAgent SDK and a CLI are all named, with plugin paths into Codex and Claude Code, and the documented call pattern is recommendation during inference plus feedback after completion. The highest stated agent-readiness in this cohort — but not behaviourally testable from our side, because login and an approved API key are required before anything can be exercised.
